excerpts.author: bridge-bot
excerpts.content:
<yoavw> > That makes sense, okay. Don't know where I got the idea that mempool clients would only forward txs for known paymasters.

It's permissionless but I can see where the confusion could come from.  Paymaster rules are more nuanced:
- If the paymaster doesn't need to access its own storage (only the account's), then it is accepted (and the UserOp is propagated). It has no way to DoS the mempool so it's equivalent to an account.
- If the paymaster does access its own storage, it could DoS the mempool by changing its behavior when used multiple times in the same bundle.  So it is only accepted and propagated if it locked a stake.  The stake serves as a sybil resistance mechanism, allowing nodes to keep a reputation and throttle paymasters that cause mass invalidations.
- A group of nodes may choose to form their own alt mempool where they waive this requirement and choose to trust a certain paymaster after auditing it. But this can't be done in the canonical mempool because the protocol is not opinionated about any specific paymaster.

I guess the confusion came from some people talking about the 3rd case.

> Either or. I'd prefer calling into the contract and leaving validation up to it, but whatever is feasible when we have to abandon ECDSA.

I think it would be important to invalidate the non-3074 use of the ECDSA key at the same time when 3074 replaces it.  Otherwise the compromised key could drain the account, bypassing the invoker. (re @SamWilsn: That makes sense, okay. Don't know where I got the idea that mempool clients would only forward txs for known paymasters.

> Does this mean abstracting the signature check to a contract, or just hardforking to add another signature scheme?

Either or. I'd prefer calling into the contract and leaving validation up to it, but whatever is feasible when we have to abandon ECDSA.)

excerpts.author: bridge-bot
excerpts.content:
<yoavw> Yes, so in 4337 that's the bundler.  The node in the AA mempool that picks the UserOp and puts it on chain (as part of a bundle).  The bundler uses an EOA, but can be QC resistant by using each EOA exactly once, so the system remains QC resistant even if Ethereum doesn't HF.

In 7560 there is no such entity, since we added it as a transaction type.  It's closer to how 2930 handled it.  So no ECDSA involved. (re @SamWilsn: I'm not familiar with the terminology. I mean the account whose balance is deducted at the start of the on-chain transaction.)

excerpts.author: bridge-bot
excerpts.content: <SamWilsn> Neat!

excerpts.author: bridge-bot
excerpts.content: <gakonst> Opt in via new eip2718 type? (re @Doganalpaslan1: Fully agree on that, R1 should be optional.)

excerpts.author: bridge-bot
excerpts.content: <gakonst> Is there strong merit behind the backdoor argument? I asked recently about it on twitter and nobody had any evidence. Genuinely curious - don't have any stake in what wins here (re @yoavw: If we tried to enshrine r1 in a way that affects accounts without opting in, some core devs might try to kill us due to the "backdoor argument")

excerpts.author: bridge-bot
excerpts.content: <yoavw> No.  Opt-in because the precompile only gets called by accounts that actively use it, so the user has chose to trust r1.  Whereas if we enshrined it as a signature accepted by 3074, then every account becomes exposed to r1 and has no way to opt out. (re @gakonst: Opt in via new eip2718 type?)

excerpts.author: bridge-bot
excerpts.content: <yoavw> IMHO it's a myth.  But see the discussion in Ethereum Magicians for example.  Some core devs feel strongly about this. (re @gakonst: Is there strong merit behind the backdoor argument? I asked recently about it on twitter and nobody had any evidence. Genuinely curious - don't have any stake in what wins here)

excerpts.author: bridge-bot
excerpts.content: <lightclient> you could have opt-in r1 control of account with 3074 though by sending a one-time k1 auth to delegate control to an r1 pubkey

excerpts.author: bridge-bot
excerpts.content: <lightclient> but you'd need the precompile regardless

excerpts.author: bridge-bot
excerpts.content: <yoavw> Right.  And if 3074 is extended to abstract the signature to a contract (rather than an enshrined scheme), which the user opts into by setting a validation contract in a singleton registry, then everything becomes opt-in. It basically adds validation abstraction to 3074. (re @lightclient: you could have opt-in r1 control of account with 3074 though by sending a one-time k1 auth to delegate control to an r1 pubkey)

excerpts.author: bridge-bot
excerpts.content: <SamWilsn> EVMMAX? 😇 (re @lightclient: but you'd need the precompile regardles)

excerpts.author: bridge-bot
excerpts.content: <yoavw> Only if it's enshrined.  If you abstract it to a validation contract, it doesn't need to be a precompile.  And besides, r1 will probably have a precompile on many L2s.  That's what @Doganalpaslan1 has been working on. (re @lightclient: but you'd need the precompile regardles)
